extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers studying American state government / political science
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and normative guidance on state executive and legislative organization circa early 20th century: removal powers, civil service classification and procedures, legislative structure and apportionment, and constitutional checks to curb corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment as a method of removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Many state constitutions provide that civil officers may be impeached; some enumerate officers, others make all executive officers liable, and some leave causes to the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes of impeachment vary (crime, misdemeanor, treason, bribery, drunkenness, malfeasance, gross immorality, extortion, neglect of duty, incompetency, misconduct). Process generally follows U.S. Constitution: lower house initiates, senate tries the case, sometimes with state supreme court judges associated (example: New York). Nebraska uses a joint legislative session and trial by supreme court judges. Effect is removal and disqualification from state office; impeached persons remain liable to ordinary courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative resolution removal (for judges and judicial officers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal by concurrent or special resolution of the state legislature is often provided for judges and judicial officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York allows removal of court of appeals judges by concurrent resolution of both houses with two-thirds of all members elected to each house concurring; other judicial officers may be removed by the senate on the governor's recommendation with two-thirds concurrence. In all cases an opportunity to be heard must be afforded the defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal by governor and senate (joint action)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common practice where chief executive and senate jointly remove officers appointed by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In states like New York, many chief state officers and commission members are appointed by governor with senate consent and removable by their joint action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal by governor alone (for appointees)
rubrics_metrics.description: In several states the governor may remove officers whom he appoints, though this power is not extensively granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, Colorado's constitution authorizes the governor to appoint and remove officers 'for incompetency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office.' New York allows suspension of certain officers during legislative recess and removal of some local officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal by the courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may try and remove certain public officers for cause in some states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some constitutions (example: Oregon) provide that incompetency, corruption, malfeasance, or delinquency in office may be tried as criminal offenses and judgment given of dismissal from office and further punishment as prescribed by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall on petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional amendment authorized recall of officers by voter petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Oregon (1908) authorized recall on petition of 25 percent of the voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of state civil service: classified vs unclassified
rubrics_metrics.description: State civil service laws divide public offices into the unclassified service and the classified service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclassified includes offices filled by election or by the legislature or by governor and senate and certain specified offices. Classified service comprises all other positions and is subdivided into competitive, non-competitive, and exempt classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive class appointment and examination standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive class positions (clerks, stenographers, engineers, accountants, etc.) are filled by examinations, promotions, and transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations must be practical and relate to matters that fairly test capacity and fitness to perform duties. Technical positions require special examinations; reliance solely on book knowledge is disallowed. Successful candidates are ranked on an eligible list; when a vacancy occurs the appointing officer must choose from the three names highest on the roll for that service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competitive class definition and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competitive class includes minor employees impracticable to include in competitive class (e.g., bakers, carpenters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments to this class are made after non-competitive examinations conducted according to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempt class definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempt class contains deputies of principal executive officers, chief clerks, and skilled and unskilled laborers not included elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These positions are excluded from competitive appointment lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and protections for removal under civil service
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil service laws generally require removal not be for political reasons but only for incompetence or insubordination, and afford the employee the right to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement of definite charges and substantiation before removal is noted as protecting employees but may retain incompetent workers; wholesale removals risk restoring the spoils system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service commission composition and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration of civil service law is typically entrusted to a state commission of three members, with political-party balance constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York's commission has three members, not more than two from the same party, appointed by governor and senate. Duties include cooperating with governor to prepare rules, classifying the service, conducting examinations, prescribing and enforcing rules, keeping records, making investigations, reporting on civil service condition, and compelling attendance of witnesses for investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on blending merit and appointing officer discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to reserve a portion of appointments to 'fitness' assigned by appointing officers (e.g., limiting merit to 50%) undermined civil service and reintroduced partisan methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience cited (Governor Black, Governor Roosevelt) shows that while experience and character matter, statutory schemes giving large discretionary shares to appointing officers caused disorganization and were abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability of competitive selection for positions of trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive examination for positions involving trust and responsibility has been demonstrated practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although heads of departments seek exemptions for confidential or fiduciary positions, New York commission testimony suggests competition largely yields beneficial results and the restrictions on choice are mainly salutary to public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service improvement practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures for improving public administration include conferences, periodical examinations of local commissions, and investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York commission held state-wide conferences to cultivate esprit de corps, promote efficiency, and discuss concrete problems; it began making periodical examinations into municipal civil service commissions to expose abuses and stimulate improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative powers and domain
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures enjoy every right and authority not expressly denied by the U.S. or state constitution, controlling civil law, criminal definitions, taxation, and the police power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They legislate on contracts, property, inheritance, corporations, marriage/divorce, crime and punishment, taxation, and public health/morals/welfare/regulation of professions and business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and procedural checks on legislative abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions incorporate various restrictions to curb legislative corruption and abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks include the governor's veto (to prevent misappropriation and hasty/corrupt legislation), restricted session lengths (e.g., 50–60 days), forbidding special/local laws except under safeguards, prescribing many substantive matters in the constitution (education, taxation, corporations), and prescribing legislative procedure to secure regularity and publicity. Some states adopt initiative and referendum systems, placing ultimate legislative power with the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral structure rationale and house differences
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures are bicameral to check hasty measures and secure careful consideration; upper houses (senates) differ from lower houses by larger districts, longer terms, and often continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senatorial districts are larger (often combining assembly districts), senators usually serve longer terms, and partial renewals may create a continuous body similar to the U.S. Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment principle: equal population and reapportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern democratic theory holds representatives should be apportioned among districts with substantially equal inhabitants and reapportioned after each census.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About one-third of states prescribe such distribution; reapportionment corrects population-caused discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions and inequalities in apportionment (county and rural protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many state constitutions make concessions that preserve minimum representation for counties or rural units, producing under- and over-representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alabama guarantees at least one member per county; Florida limits members per county; New York grants each county (except Hamilton) at least one assembly member, creating districts that fall far below population ratios. Discrimination against cities in favor of rural districts causes 'rotten boroughs' (examples: Connecticut, Vermont), yielding gross inequalities and underrepresentation of populous urban centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional prescription of legislative membership size
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions commonly prescribe the number of legislative members to prevent the legislature from increasing its own size for political purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows it is wise to fix membership in the constitution rather than leave the legislature free to change its size.
